notes.h: Atomic structure, bonding and the bond-energy curve
notes.body:
Properties of engineering materials trace back to how atoms are bonded. Electronegativity (Pauling scale) measures how strongly an atom attracts shared electrons; the difference Δχ between two elements predicts the bond type.

Primary bonds (roughly 100–1000 kJ/mol):
- Ionic: electron transfer between atoms with large Δχ (NaCl, MgO). Non-directional but charge balance must be kept, so ionic solids are hard, brittle and poor electrical conductors as solids.
- Covalent: shared electron pairs, strongly directional (diamond, Si, SiC, C–C bonds in polymer chains). Very high stiffness and melting point; brittle.
- Metallic: positive ion cores in a delocalised electron "sea". Non-directional, so dislocations move easily: metals are ductile and conduct heat and electricity well.

Secondary bonds (roughly 1–50 kJ/mol) arise from dipoles: London dispersion (fluctuating dipoles), permanent dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonding (H bonded to N, O or F). In polymers these act between chains, so they control Tg, Tm and stiffness.

A common estimate of ionic character is %IC = 100[1 − exp(−0.25Δχ²)]. Most real bonds are mixed.

The bond-energy curve
Net potential energy is often modelled as E(r) = −A/r + B/rⁿ, with an attractive term and a short-range repulsive term (n typically 6–12). The force is F = −dE/dr.
- Equilibrium spacing r₀ is where F = 0 (the minimum of E).
- Bond energy E₀ (depth of the well) correlates with melting point and sublimation energy.
- Curvature at r₀, S₀ = d²E/dr², is the bond stiffness; Young's modulus scales roughly as E ≈ S₀/r₀.
- Asymmetry of the well (steeper on the repulsive side) causes thermal expansion: deep, symmetric wells give low expansion coefficients.

Worked example
NaCl: Δχ = 3.16 − 0.93 = 2.23, so %IC = 100[1 − exp(−0.25 × 4.97)] ≈ 71%. MgO: Δχ = 2.13, %IC ≈ 68%. Both are predominantly but not purely ionic.

For E(r) = −A/r + B/rⁿ, setting dE/dr = 0 gives B = A·r₀ⁿ⁻¹/n and E₀ = −(A/r₀)(1 − 1/n). With A = 1.44 eV·nm, n = 8 and r₀ = 0.28 nm, E₀ = −5.14 × 0.875 ≈ −4.5 eV.

Typical moduli follow bonding: diamond about 1000 GPa, steel about 210 GPa, aluminium about 70 GPa, polyethylene below about 1 GPa because loading stretches the weak inter-chain bonds.

Exam pitfalls
- Mixing up energy and force curves: r₀ is at the energy minimum and at zero force, not at maximum force.
- Saying stiffness depends on the depth of the well; it depends on the curvature (although deep wells usually also have high curvature).
- Calling hydrogen bonds primary bonds. They are strong secondary bonds.
- Forgetting the sign convention: bond energy is negative relative to separated atoms.

notes.h: Crystal structures, Miller indices and defects
notes.body:
A crystal is a regular three-dimensional array of atoms described by a lattice plus a motif; the smallest repeating block is the unit cell, with lattice parameter a.

Three structures cover most engineering metals:
- FCC (Cu, Al, Ni, austenite): 4 atoms per cell, coordination number (CN) 12, a = 2√2R, atomic packing factor (APF) 0.74. Close-packed planes are {111}.
- BCC (α-Fe, Cr, W, Mo): 2 atoms per cell, CN 8, a = 4R/√3, APF 0.68. No truly close-packed plane; densest are {110}.
- HCP (Mg, Ti at room temperature, Zn): CN 12, APF 0.74, ideal c/a = 1.633.

Theoretical density: ρ = nA/(V_c N_A), where n is atoms per cell, A the molar mass and V_c = a³ for cubic cells.

Miller indices: take intercepts in units of a, invert, clear fractions. Directions use [uvw] and families ⟨uvw⟩; planes use (hkl) and families {hkl}. For cubic crystals the interplanar spacing is d = a/√(h² + k² + l²). Bragg's law, nλ = 2d sin θ, links X-ray diffraction peaks to d.

Slip occurs on the densest planes in the densest directions. FCC has 12 {111}⟨110⟩ systems, which is why FCC metals stay ductile at low temperature. HCP has only 3 basal systems at room temperature, so pure Mg, Zn and Cd are less ductile.

Defects
- Point: vacancies, self-interstitials, substitutional and interstitial solute atoms. Equilibrium vacancy fraction N_v/N = exp(−Q_v/kT), with T in kelvin.
- Line: edge and screw dislocations, characterised by the Burgers vector b (perpendicular to the line for edge, parallel for screw). Dislocation glide lets crystals yield at a small fraction of the theoretical shear strength.
- Planar: grain boundaries, twin boundaries, stacking faults, free surfaces.
- Volume: pores, cracks, inclusions.

Hume-Rothery rules for extensive substitutional solid solubility: atomic radii within about 15%, same crystal structure, similar electronegativity, similar valence. Cu–Ni satisfies all four and is fully miscible.

Worked example
Copper (FCC, R = 0.128 nm, A = 63.55 g/mol): a = 2√2 × 0.128 = 0.362 nm, V_c = 4.75 × 10⁻²³ cm³. ρ = (4 × 63.55)/(4.75 × 10⁻²³ × 6.022 × 10²³) ≈ 8.90 g/cm³, close to the measured 8.96 g/cm³. d₁₁₁ = 0.362/√3 = 0.209 nm; with Cu-Kα (λ = 0.1542 nm), sin θ = 0.369, so the (111) peak is at 2θ ≈ 43.3°.

Exam pitfalls
- Wrong atom counts: corners count 1/8, faces 1/2, body centre 1.
- Using °C in the Arrhenius term instead of kelvin, or mixing k (eV/K) with molar Q (use R).
- Not clearing fractions or forgetting that an intercept at infinity gives index 0.
- Assuming the most close-packed structure is always the most ductile; slip-system count and their activity matter.

Engineering stress σ = F/A₀ and engineering strain ε = ΔL/L₀. In the elastic region Hooke's law gives σ = Eε. Poisson's ratio ν = −ε_lateral/ε_axial (about 0.3 for metals), and for isotropic materials G = E/[2(1 + ν)].

The tensile test (BS EN ISO 6892-1) gives:
- Yield strength, or 0.2% proof stress where yielding is gradual.
- Ultimate tensile strength (UTS): maximum engineering stress, where necking starts.
- Ductility: percentage elongation after fracture, and reduction of area (RA) = (A₀ − A_f)/A₀.
- Resilience (elastic energy per volume) U_r = σ_y²/2E; toughness is the total area under the curve.

True stress and strain: σ_T = σ(1 + ε) and ε_T = ln(1 + ε), valid only up to necking (uniform deformation). Plastic flow often follows Hollomon's law σ_T = Kε_Tⁿ; Considère's criterion places necking where dσ_T/dε_T = σ_T, which gives ε_T = n at necking.

Hardness: Brinell, Vickers (HV = 1.854F/d² with F in kgf and d the mean diagonal in mm), Rockwell. For steels, UTS (MPa) ≈ 3.45 × HB is a useful rough link. Charpy impact testing (BS EN ISO 148-1) measures absorbed energy; BCC steels show a ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (DBTT), while FCC metals generally do not.

Strengthening mechanisms all work by obstructing dislocation motion:
- Grain refinement: Hall–Petch σ_y = σ₀ + k d^(−1/2). The only mechanism that also improves toughness.
- Solid solution strengthening: lattice strain fields around solute atoms.
- Work (strain) hardening: rising dislocation density; reversed by annealing.
- Precipitation and dispersion strengthening: fine particles cut or bypassed (Orowan looping).

Critical resolved shear stress: Schmid's law τ_R = σ cos φ cos λ, where φ is the angle between load axis and slip-plane normal and λ the angle between load axis and slip direction. Yield begins when τ_R reaches τ_CRSS; cos φ cos λ peaks at 0.5.

Worked example
A 10 mm diameter bar (A₀ = 78.5 mm², gauge 50 mm) yields at 23.6 kN and reaches 35.3 kN. σ_y = 300 MPa; UTS = 449 MPa. If the final length is 61.5 mm and the neck diameter 6.2 mm, elongation = 23% and RA = 1 − 0.62² = 62%. With E = 207 GPa, U_r = 300²/(2 × 207 000) ≈ 0.22 MJ/m³.

Hall–Petch: σ₀ = 70 MPa, k = 0.74 MPa·m^½, d = 25 µm gives σ_y = 70 + 0.74/0.005 = 218 MPa.

Exam pitfalls
- Using true-stress formulae beyond the onset of necking.
- Reading the drop after UTS as material weakening; it reflects falling cross-section.
- Quoting elongation without a gauge length; it depends on L₀.
- Confusing toughness (energy) with strength (stress) or hardness.

notes.h: Phase diagrams, the lever rule and the Fe–C system
notes.body:
A phase is a homogeneous region of uniform structure and composition. Equilibrium phase diagrams show the stable phases at each composition and temperature, assuming slow cooling.

Gibbs phase rule: F = C − P + 2. At fixed pressure (usual for condensed systems) F = C − P + 1. In a binary system, a three-phase point such as a eutectic has F = 2 − 3 + 1 = 0: it is invariant.

Reading a two-phase region:
- Draw a horizontal tie line at the temperature of interest; its ends give each phase's composition.
- Lever rule: the fraction of phase α is W_α = (C_β − C₀)/(C_β − C_α), where C₀ is the overall alloy composition. Each phase is weighted by the length of the opposite arm.

Diagram types
- Isomorphous (Cu–Ni): complete solid solubility; fast cooling gives cored dendrites.
- Binary eutectic (Pb–Sn): eutectic at 61.9 wt% Sn and 183 °C, with α at 18.3 wt% Sn and β at 97.8 wt% Sn. Eutectic alloys solidify at one temperature to fine lamellar α + β, ideal for solders.

Invariant reactions on cooling:
- Eutectic: L → α + β
- Eutectoid: γ → α + β (all solid)
- Peritectic: L + α → β

The Fe–Fe₃C diagram (Fe₃C is metastable; graphite is the true equilibrium phase but forms slowly)
- Eutectoid: 0.76 wt% C at 727 °C, austenite (γ, FCC) → ferrite (α, BCC) + cementite (Fe₃C), giving lamellar pearlite.
- Eutectic: 4.30 wt% C at 1147 °C (basis of cast irons).
- Maximum C in ferrite 0.022 wt% (727 °C); in austenite 2.14 wt% (1147 °C). Cementite contains 6.70 wt% C.
- Hypoeutectoid steels (< 0.76% C) form proeutectoid ferrite then pearlite; hypereutectoid steels form embrittling proeutectoid cementite on prior austenite grain boundaries.

Worked example: 0.40 wt% C steel cooled slowly
Just above 727 °C: proeutectoid ferrite (0.022% C) plus austenite (0.76% C). Pearlite fraction W_p = (0.40 − 0.022)/(0.76 − 0.022) = 0.51; proeutectoid ferrite = 0.49.
Just below 727 °C, total ferrite = (6.70 − 0.40)/(6.70 − 0.022) = 0.94 and total Fe₃C = 0.06. Within pearlite itself, Fe₃C ≈ (0.76 − 0.022)/(6.70 − 0.022) ≈ 0.11.

Exam pitfalls
- Inverting the lever rule (using the near arm instead of the far arm).
- Confusing phases with microconstituents: pearlite is a microconstituent made of two phases.
- Applying the diagram to rapidly cooled material; martensite and bainite do not appear on it.
- Reading phase compositions from C₀ rather than the tie-line ends.

Ferrous alloys dominate tonnage: plain carbon steels (low < ~0.25% C, medium, high), low-alloy steels, stainless steels (at least about 10.5 wt% Cr, forming a passive Cr₂O₃ film) and cast irons (> 2.14% C). Key non-ferrous families are aluminium alloys (low density, age-hardenable series), titanium alloys (high specific strength, corrosion resistance), copper alloys and nickel superalloys (creep resistance).

Diffusion underpins heat treatment. Fick's first law J = −D dC/dx (steady state); Fick's second law ∂C/∂t = D ∂²C/∂x². For a semi-infinite solid with constant surface concentration: (C_x − C₀)/(C_s − C₀) = 1 − erf[x/(2√(Dt))]. D = D₀ exp(−Q_d/RT), so diffusion is strongly temperature dependent. Penetration depth scales with √(Dt).

Heat treatment of steels
- Full annealing: austenitise, furnace cool, giving coarse pearlite, soft and ductile.
- Normalising: austenitise, air cool, giving finer pearlite and refined grains.
- Hardening: austenitise and quench to form martensite, a supersaturated body-centred tetragonal phase formed by a diffusionless shear transformation. Its hardness rises with carbon content.
- Tempering: reheat below 727 °C to form tempered martensite (fine carbides in ferrite), trading hardness for toughness.
- Austempering gives bainite; martempering reduces distortion and quench cracking.

TTT (isothermal) and CCT (continuous cooling) diagrams show transformation kinetics. Alloying elements such as Cr, Mo, Ni and Mn shift the curves to longer times, raising hardenability: the depth to which martensite forms on quenching. It is measured with the Jominy end-quench test. Hardenability is not hardness.

Surface hardening: carburising (C diffuses into austenite), nitriding (lower temperature, ferrite), induction or flame hardening (surface heat then quench).

Precipitation hardening (e.g. Al–Cu): solution treat in the single-phase α field, quench to a supersaturated solid solution, then age. The precipitation sequence is GP zones → θ″ → θ′ → θ (CuAl₂). Peak strength comes from fine coherent or semi-coherent precipitates; overageing coarsens them and strength falls.

Worked example: carburising
Steel with 0.20 wt% C, surface held at 1.00 wt% C, 1000 °C. Target: 0.50 wt% C at 0.5 mm. D = 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ exp(−148 000/(8.314 × 1273)) = 1.94 × 10⁻¹¹ m²/s.
(0.50 − 0.20)/(1.00 − 0.20) = 0.375, so erf(z) = 0.625 and z ≈ 0.627.
t = [x/(2z)]²/D = (0.5 × 10⁻³/1.254)²/1.94 × 10⁻¹¹ ≈ 8.2 × 10³ s ≈ 2.3 h.

Exam pitfalls
- Treating martensite as an equilibrium phase or placing it on the Fe–C diagram.
- Confusing hardenability with maximum hardness.
- Using °C in Arrhenius expressions.
- Forgetting the quench step in age hardening, or assuming longer ageing always strengthens.

Polymers
Long-chain molecules with covalent backbones and secondary bonds between chains.
- Thermoplastics (PE, PP, PVC, PA, PET): linear or branched chains that soften on heating and can be remelted.
- Thermosets (epoxy, phenolic): covalently cross-linked networks that cannot be remelted.
- Elastomers: lightly cross-linked, used above Tg, giving large recoverable strain.

Chain length: degree of polymerisation DP = M_n/m, where m is the repeat-unit molar mass. Number-average M_n weights by number of chains; weight-average M_w ≥ M_n, and the dispersity M_w/M_n ≥ 1. Crystallinity rises with linear, regular (isotactic or syndiotactic) chains and slow cooling:
% crystallinity = ρ_c(ρ_s − ρ_a)/[ρ_s(ρ_c − ρ_a)] × 100.
The glass transition Tg marks the change from glassy to rubbery behaviour in amorphous regions; crystalline regions melt at Tm. Polymers are viscoelastic: their stiffness depends on time and temperature, and they creep at room temperature.

Ceramics
Ionic or covalent compounds (Al₂O₃, SiC, Si₃N₄, ZrO₂) and glasses. They have high stiffness, hardness and melting points, and good compressive strength, but low fracture toughness. Strength is controlled by the largest flaw, so it varies widely between nominally identical parts. The Weibull model gives survival probability P_s = exp[−(V/V₀)(σ/σ₀)ᵐ]. A high Weibull modulus m means less scatter; engineering ceramics are often around 5–20. Larger components are more likely to contain a critical flaw.

Composites
A matrix (polymer, metal or ceramic) with a reinforcement (particles, short or continuous fibres) or a structural form (laminates, sandwich panels).
- Longitudinal (iso-strain) rule of mixtures: E_∥ = V_f E_f + V_m E_m.
- Transverse (iso-stress): 1/E_⊥ = V_f/E_f + V_m/E_m.
- Critical fibre length l_c = σ_f d/(2τ_c): fibres much longer than l_c carry close to their full strength.
Laminates use stacked plies at different angles (e.g. 0/±45/90) to approach in-plane isotropy.

Worked example
Carbon fibre (230 GPa) in epoxy (3.5 GPa), V_f = 0.6:
E_∥ = 0.6 × 230 + 0.4 × 3.5 = 139 GPa.
E_⊥ = 1/(0.6/230 + 0.4/3.5) = 8.6 GPa.
The 16-fold anisotropy shows why ply orientation is the central design variable. With fibre strength 3.5 GPa, d = 7 µm and τ_c = 50 MPa, l_c = 3500 × 7 × 10⁻⁶/(2 × 50) = 0.245 mm.

Weibull: σ₀ = 300 MPa, m = 10. At 200 MPa, P_s = exp[−(2/3)¹⁰] ≈ 0.983; at 250 MPa, P_s ≈ 0.851.

Exam pitfalls
- Applying the longitudinal rule to transverse loading.
- Saying thermosets melt, or that cross-linking makes elastomers rigid.
- Quoting a single strength for a ceramic without a probability or volume.
- Confusing Tg with Tm; fully amorphous polymers have no Tm.

Fracture
- Ductile fracture: plastic deformation, necking, microvoid nucleation and coalescence, giving cup-and-cone surfaces with dimples.
- Brittle fracture: little plasticity; transgranular cleavage (flat facets, river marks) or intergranular fracture.

Griffith showed that for an ideally brittle solid, σ_f = √(2Eγ_s/πa). Linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM) uses the stress intensity factor K = Yσ√(πa), where Y is a geometry factor (about 1.12 for a shallow edge crack). Fast fracture occurs when K reaches the plane-strain fracture toughness K_IC. A valid K_IC test (ASTM E399) needs thickness B ≥ 2.5(K_IC/σ_y)². Thinner sections fail at a higher, thickness-dependent K_c.

Fatigue
Failure under cyclic stress below the static strength: initiation (usually at surface stress concentrations), stable growth (beach marks, striations), then final fast fracture.
- S–N curves: many steels show an endurance (fatigue) limit; aluminium alloys do not, so a fatigue strength at a stated life is quoted.
- Mean stress: Goodman σ_a = σ_e(1 − σ_m/σ_UTS). Gerber (parabolic) and Soderberg (based on yield) are alternatives.
- Variable amplitude: Palmgren–Miner rule, Σnᵢ/Nᵢ = 1 at failure.
- Crack growth: Paris law da/dN = C(ΔK)ᵐ, with m typically about 2–4 for metals.
- Stress concentration at an elliptical notch: K_t = 1 + 2√(a/ρ).
Remedies include smooth fillets, good surface finish, shot peening (compressive residual stress) and avoiding sharp section changes.

Creep
Time-dependent deformation at constant load, significant above about 0.4 T_m (absolute). Curves show primary (decreasing rate), secondary (steady state) and tertiary (accelerating, with necking and cavities) stages.
- Steady-state rate: ε̇ = Aσⁿ exp(−Q_c/RT). Dislocation (power-law) creep has n ≈ 3–8; diffusional creep (Nabarro–Herring through grains, Coble along boundaries) has n ≈ 1 and dominates at low stress and fine grain size.
- Larson–Miller parameter P = T(C + log₁₀ t_r), with T in K, t_r in hours and C ≈ 20, links temperature and rupture life.
Creep-resistant design uses high-T_m alloys, solid-solution and precipitate strengthening (γ′ in nickel superalloys), coarse grains or directionally solidified and single-crystal turbine blades.

Worked example: Paris law
Δσ = 150 MPa (R = 0, so σ_max = 150 MPa), Y = 1, C = 1 × 10⁻¹¹ (m/cycle, MPa√m), m = 3, K_IC = 50 MPa√m, a₀ = 1 mm.
Critical size: a_f = (K_IC/σ_max)²/π = 35.4 mm.
Integrating da/[C(Δσ√(πa))³] gives N = 2(a₀^(−½) − a_f^(−½))/[C(Δσ√π)³] ≈ 2.8 × 10⁵ cycles.

Exam pitfalls
- Using σ_max instead of Δσ in the Paris law, or forgetting the critical crack length depends on σ_max.
- Applying LEFM where there is extensive yielding.
- Using °C in Larson–Miller or creep rate equations.
- Assuming aluminium has an endurance limit.

Materials selection matches the requirements of a component to material properties systematically. Ashby's method has four steps:
- Translation: state the function (what it does), objective (what to minimise or maximise, e.g. mass or cost), constraints (non-negotiable conditions such as a required stiffness, or service temperature) and free variables (e.g. a cross-section dimension).
- Screening: remove materials that fail any constraint (temperature, corrosion, electrical insulation).
- Ranking: order the survivors using a material index derived from the objective and constraints.
- Documentation: research the top candidates in depth (processing, joining, supply, experience, environmental record).

Deriving an index: a light, stiff beam
A square beam of side b, length L, must reach bending stiffness S = C₁EI/L³ with I = b⁴/12. The free variable b is eliminated using mass m = b²Lρ:
m = (12S/C₁)^½ L^(5/2) × (ρ/E^½).
Mass is minimised by maximising M = E^½/ρ.

Common indices (maximise):
- Light, stiff tie: E/ρ
- Light, stiff beam: E^½/ρ
- Light, stiff panel (plate): E^⅓/ρ
- Light, strong tie: σ_f/ρ
- Light, strong beam: σ_f^⅔/ρ
- Light, strong panel: σ_f^½/ρ
To minimise cost instead, replace ρ with C_mρ, where C_m is cost per kg.

Selection charts plot two properties on log scales. An index M = E^(1/x)/ρ plots as a straight line of slope x on an E–ρ chart; moving the line towards the top left leaves only materials with higher M.

Further tools
- Multiple constraints: calculate the mass required by each constraint; the larger value is the active one for that material.
- Conflicting objectives: trade-off plots and penalty (value) functions such as Z = α₁m + α₂C.
- Shape factors: I-beams and tubes raise bending efficiency, but each material can only be made into certain shapes.
- Damage tolerance: yield-before-break favours high K_IC/σ_y; leak-before-break favours high K_IC²/σ_y.

Worked example
Light, stiff beam (E in GPa, ρ in Mg/m³): steel (210, 7.85) M = 1.85; aluminium (69, 2.70) M = 3.08; CFRP (100, 1.55) M = 6.45. Relative to steel, mass falls to 0.60 for aluminium and 0.29 for CFRP. For a tie, E/ρ is 26.8 for steel and 25.6 for aluminium, almost identical, so aluminium saves no mass in a stiffness-limited tie. Shape of loading changes the answer.

Exam pitfalls
- Ranking by a single property (E or σ_f) instead of the index.
- Treating a fixed dimension as a free variable, which changes the exponent.
- Forgetting to screen for constraints before ranking.
- Ignoring manufacturing, joining and cost, which documentation must address.

cards.f: What determines whether a bond is mainly ionic or covalent?
cards.b: The electronegativity difference Δχ between the atoms. A large Δχ favours electron transfer (ionic); a small Δχ favours electron sharing (covalent).

cards.f: Why are metals ductile while ionic ceramics are brittle?
cards.b: Metallic bonding is non-directional, so dislocations glide without disrupting bonding. In ionic solids slip would bring like charges together, and covalent bonds are directional, so dislocation motion is very difficult.

cards.f: Formula for percentage ionic character from electronegativities
cards.b: %IC = 100[1 − exp(−0.25Δχ²)]. For NaCl, Δχ = 2.23 gives about 71%.

cards.f: At the equilibrium spacing r₀, what are the values of net force and potential energy?
cards.b: Net force is zero and potential energy is at its minimum, equal to the bond energy E₀.

cards.f: Which feature of the bond-energy curve controls Young's modulus?
cards.b: Its curvature at r₀: the bond stiffness S₀ = d²E/dr². Young's modulus scales roughly as S₀/r₀.

cards.f: Why do materials with deep, symmetric energy wells have low thermal expansion?
cards.b: Expansion comes from the asymmetry of the well: as vibration amplitude rises, the mean spacing shifts outward. A deep, symmetric well limits that shift.

cards.f: Name the three types of secondary bond in order of increasing typical strength.
cards.b: London dispersion (fluctuating dipoles), permanent dipole–dipole interactions, and hydrogen bonds.

cards.f: Why is polyethylene's modulus so much lower than diamond's when both have C–C bonds?
cards.b: In polyethylene, much of the deformation stretches the weak van der Waals bonds between chains. In diamond every load path runs through covalent bonds.

cards.f: For E(r) = −A/r + B/rⁿ, give B and E₀ in terms of A, n and r₀.
cards.b: Setting dE/dr = 0 gives B = A·r₀ⁿ⁻¹/n and E₀ = −(A/r₀)(1 − 1/n).

cards.f: FCC: atoms per cell, coordination number, APF, a in terms of R
cards.b: 4 atoms, CN 12, APF 0.74, a = 2√2R.

cards.f: BCC: atoms per cell, coordination number, APF, a in terms of R
cards.b: 2 atoms, CN 8, APF 0.68, a = 4R/√3.

cards.f: Theoretical density formula for a crystal
cards.b: ρ = nA/(V_c N_A): atoms per cell × molar mass, divided by cell volume × Avogadro's number.

cards.f: Interplanar spacing for cubic crystals
cards.b: d_hkl = a/√(h² + k² + l²). Combine it with Bragg's law nλ = 2d sin θ to index diffraction peaks.

cards.f: Slip systems in FCC metals
cards.b: {111}⟨110⟩: 4 planes × 3 directions = 12 systems, which keeps FCC metals ductile even at cryogenic temperatures.

cards.f: Edge versus screw dislocation: Burgers vector orientation
cards.b: Edge: b is perpendicular to the dislocation line. Screw: b is parallel to the line. Mixed dislocations have both components.

cards.f: Equilibrium vacancy fraction
cards.b: N_v/N = exp(−Q_v/kT), with T in kelvin. It rises sharply with temperature, which is why diffusion is fast near the melting point.

cards.f: State the Hume-Rothery rules for extensive substitutional solubility.
cards.b: Atomic radii within about 15%, same crystal structure, similar electronegativity and similar valence.

cards.f: Why is pure magnesium (HCP) less ductile at room temperature than aluminium (FCC)?
cards.b: Mg has only 3 easily activated basal slip systems, fewer than the 5 independent systems needed for general polycrystal deformation (von Mises criterion). Al has 12 {111}⟨110⟩ systems.

cards.f: Define 0.2% proof stress.
cards.b: The stress at which a line parallel to the elastic portion, offset by 0.2% strain, cuts the stress–strain curve. It is used when yielding is gradual.

cards.f: True stress and true strain in terms of engineering values
cards.b: σ_T = σ(1 + ε) and ε_T = ln(1 + ε). They hold only up to the onset of necking.

cards.f: Considère's criterion and its result for a Hollomon material
cards.b: Necking starts when dσ_T/dε_T = σ_T. For σ_T = Kε_Tⁿ, this gives true uniform strain ε_T = n.

cards.f: Hall–Petch equation
cards.b: σ_y = σ₀ + k d^(−1/2). Grain refinement raises yield strength and, unlike other mechanisms, usually improves toughness too.

cards.f: Schmid's law
cards.b: τ_R = σ cos φ cos λ, where φ is the angle between load axis and slip-plane normal and λ between load axis and slip direction. Slip begins when τ_R = τ_CRSS.

cards.f: Modulus of resilience
cards.b: U_r = σ_y²/2E: the elastic strain energy stored per unit volume up to yield.

cards.f: Relationship between E, G and ν for an isotropic material
cards.b: G = E/[2(1 + ν)]. For steel (E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.3), G ≈ 77 GPa.

cards.f: Why do BCC steels show a ductile-to-brittle transition but FCC metals generally do not?
cards.b: In BCC metals the yield stress rises steeply as temperature falls, until it exceeds the cleavage fracture stress. In FCC metals yield stress is much less temperature sensitive.

cards.f: Vickers hardness formula
cards.b: HV = 1.854F/d², with F in kgf and d the mean indent diagonal in mm. For 30 kgf and d = 0.40 mm, HV ≈ 348.

cards.f: Gibbs phase rule at constant pressure
cards.b: F = C − P + 1. At a binary eutectic point P = 3, so F = 0 (invariant).

cards.f: Lever rule for phase α in an α + β field
cards.b: W_α = (C_β − C₀)/(C_β − C_α): the arm opposite the phase, divided by the whole tie line.

cards.f: Write the eutectic, eutectoid and peritectic reactions on cooling.
cards.b: Eutectic L → α + β; eutectoid γ → α + β; peritectic L + α → β.

cards.f: Fe–Fe₃C eutectoid composition and temperature
cards.b: 0.76 wt% C at 727 °C: austenite → ferrite + cementite (pearlite).

cards.f: Pb–Sn eutectic point
cards.b: 61.9 wt% Sn at 183 °C, with α at 18.3 wt% Sn and β at 97.8 wt% Sn.

cards.f: Phase versus microconstituent
cards.b: A phase is homogeneous in structure and composition. A microconstituent is a recognisable feature that may contain more than one phase, e.g. pearlite (ferrite + Fe₃C).

cards.f: Pearlite fraction in a slowly cooled 0.40 wt% C steel
cards.b: W_p = (0.40 − 0.022)/(0.76 − 0.022) ≈ 0.51; the rest (0.49) is proeutectoid ferrite.

cards.f: What is coring and why does it occur?
cards.b: Composition gradients within dendrites because solid-state diffusion cannot keep pace with non-equilibrium cooling. The cores are richer in the higher-melting component.

cards.f: Why is Fe₃C described as metastable?
cards.b: Graphite plus ferrite is the true equilibrium state, but cementite forms far faster, so it persists indefinitely at room temperature. Si promotes graphite in grey cast irons.

cards.f: What is martensite?
cards.b: A supersaturated body-centred tetragonal Fe–C phase formed by diffusionless shear when austenite is cooled fast enough to avoid pearlite and bainite. It is very hard and brittle.

cards.f: Normalising versus full annealing
cards.b: Both austenitise first. Normalising air-cools to fine pearlite and refined grains; annealing furnace-cools to coarse, softer pearlite.

cards.f: Hardenability versus hardness
cards.b: Hardness is resistance to indentation, controlled mainly by carbon content in martensite. Hardenability is the depth to which martensite can form on quenching, raised by alloying elements.

cards.f: What does the Jominy end-quench test measure?
cards.b: Hardness along a bar quenched at one end, giving hardness against cooling rate (distance), which characterises hardenability.

cards.f: Erf solution of Fick's second law (constant surface concentration)
cards.b: (C_x − C₀)/(C_s − C₀) = 1 − erf[x/(2√(Dt))], for a semi-infinite solid.

cards.f: Steps in precipitation hardening
cards.b: Solution treat in the single-phase field, quench to a supersaturated solid solution, then age (naturally or artificially) to form fine precipitates.

cards.f: Precipitation sequence in Al–Cu
cards.b: Supersaturated α → GP zones → θ″ → θ′ → θ (CuAl₂). Peak hardness corresponds to fine θ″/θ′; coarse θ means overaged.

cards.f: Why temper martensite?
cards.b: As-quenched martensite is too brittle. Tempering precipitates fine carbides and relieves stresses, trading some hardness for toughness.

cards.f: If carburising depth scales with √(Dt), how does time change for double the case depth at constant temperature?
cards.b: Time increases fourfold, because x ∝ √(Dt) gives t ∝ x².

cards.f: Thermoplastic versus thermoset
cards.b: Thermoplastics have linear or branched chains held by secondary bonds and can be remelted. Thermosets are covalently cross-linked networks that degrade rather than melt.

cards.f: Degree of polymerisation
cards.b: DP = M_n/m. Polyethylene with M_n = 100 000 g/mol (m = 28.05 g/mol) has DP ≈ 3570.

cards.f: Percentage crystallinity from densities
cards.b: %C = ρ_c(ρ_s − ρ_a)/[ρ_s(ρ_c − ρ_a)] × 100, with c = crystalline, a = amorphous, s = sample.

cards.f: What is the glass transition temperature?
cards.b: The temperature at which amorphous regions change from rigid and glassy to rubbery as segmental chain motion becomes possible. Modulus falls by orders of magnitude.

cards.f: Weibull survival probability
cards.b: P_s = exp[−(V/V₀)(σ/σ₀)ᵐ]. A higher modulus m means less strength scatter and more predictable components.

cards.f: Longitudinal and transverse rules of mixtures
cards.b: E_∥ = V_fE_f + V_mE_m (iso-strain). 1/E_⊥ = V_f/E_f + V_m/E_m (iso-stress).

cards.f: Critical fibre length
cards.b: l_c = σ_f d/(2τ_c). Fibres much longer than l_c can be loaded close to their strength through interfacial shear.

cards.f: Why does a large ceramic part have lower expected strength than a small one?
cards.b: A larger stressed volume is more likely to contain a large critical flaw, so its survival probability at a given stress is lower.

cards.f: Why do semicrystalline polymers stay useful above Tg while amorphous ones do not?
cards.b: The crystalline regions remain intact up to Tm and act as physical cross-links, keeping some stiffness. Amorphous polymers soften to rubber or flow above Tg.

cards.f: Stress intensity factor
cards.b: K = Yσ√(πa), with Y a geometry factor (about 1.12 for a shallow edge crack). Fast fracture occurs when K = K_IC.

cards.f: Griffith equation for a brittle solid
cards.b: σ_f = √(2Eγ_s/πa), where γ_s is the surface energy and a the crack half-length (or edge crack depth).

cards.f: Plane-strain validity condition for K_IC testing
cards.b: Thickness B, crack length a and the uncracked ligament (W − a) must each be at least 2.5(K_IC/σ_y)², per ASTM E399.

cards.f: Goodman relation
cards.b: σ_a = σ_e(1 − σ_m/σ_UTS): permissible alternating stress falls linearly with mean stress.

cards.f: Palmgren–Miner rule
cards.b: Failure is predicted when Σnᵢ/Nᵢ = 1. It ignores load sequence effects.

cards.f: Paris law
cards.b: da/dN = C(ΔK)ᵐ, describing stable fatigue crack growth in the intermediate ΔK regime.

cards.f: Features of a fatigue fracture surface
cards.b: Initiation site (often at the surface), beach marks visible by eye, microscopic striations, and a rough final fast-fracture region.

cards.f: Larson–Miller parameter
cards.b: P = T(C + log₁₀ t_r), with T in K, t_r in h and C ≈ 20. Short high-temperature tests can then predict long life at lower temperature.

cards.f: Dislocation creep versus diffusional creep
cards.b: Dislocation (power-law) creep: n ≈ 3–8, high stress. Diffusional creep (Nabarro–Herring, Coble): n ≈ 1, low stress and fine grains.

cards.f: Four steps of Ashby's selection method
cards.b: Translation, screening, ranking, documentation.

cards.f: Distinguish function, objective, constraint and free variable.
cards.b: Function: what the part does. Objective: quantity to minimise or maximise. Constraint: condition that must be met. Free variable: a parameter the designer may change.

cards.f: Index for a light, stiff beam
cards.b: M = E^½/ρ (maximise), derived by fixing stiffness and length and freeing the section size.

cards.f: Index for a light, stiff panel
cards.b: M = E^⅓/ρ, with plate thickness the free variable.

cards.f: Index for a light, strong beam
cards.b: M = σ_f^⅔/ρ.

cards.f: How do you convert a minimum-mass index into a minimum-cost index?
cards.b: Replace ρ by C_mρ, where C_m is cost per kilogram, e.g. E^½/(C_mρ).

cards.f: On a log E–log ρ chart, what slope has a line of constant E^½/ρ?
cards.b: Slope 2, since log E = 2 log ρ + 2 log M.

cards.f: Yield-before-break and leak-before-break indices
cards.b: Yield-before-break: maximise K_IC/σ_y. Leak-before-break: maximise K_IC²/σ_y.

cards.f: Why does aluminium save little mass over steel for a stiffness-limited tie?
cards.b: E/ρ is nearly equal for the two (about 27 and 26 GPa per Mg/m³). Aluminium's advantage appears in bending and panels, where the indices weight density more strongly.

questions.q: Which bonding mainly holds neighbouring polyethylene chains together?
questions.why: Bonds along each chain are covalent, but chains are attached to each other by weak dispersion forces, which is why PE is soft and melts at low temperature.

questions.q: A material's coefficient of thermal expansion is mainly linked to which feature of its interatomic potential energy curve?
options: The depth of the energy well
The asymmetry of the energy well
The slope of the attractive term at large r
questions.why: As atoms vibrate more strongly, the asymmetric well moves their mean separation outward. Depth links to melting point and curvature to stiffness.

questions.q: How many atoms belong to one FCC unit cell, and what is its coordination number?
questions.why: 8 corners × 1/8 + 6 faces × 1/2 = 4 atoms, and each atom has 12 nearest neighbours.

questions.q: A specimen is stretched uniformly to an engineering strain of 0.20. What is the true strain?
questions.why: ε_T = ln(1 + 0.20) = 0.182. The true strain is always below the engineering strain in tension.

questions.q: Vickers test: 30 kgf load, mean indent diagonal 0.40 mm. What is the hardness?
For a binary alloy at fixed pressure, how many degrees of freedom are there at the eutectic point?
questions.why: F = C − P + 1 = 2 − 3 + 1 = 0. Temperature and all three phase compositions are fixed.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of tempering a quenched medium-carbon steel?
options: To convert retained ferrite into martensite
To improve toughness by forming fine carbides in ferrite, at some cost in hardness
questions.why: Tempering reheats martensite below the eutectoid temperature to form tempered martensite: tougher, slightly less hard.

questions.q: A unidirectional composite is loaded perpendicular to its fibres. Which model gives the best simple estimate of its modulus?
questions.why: Transverse loading is approximately iso-stress (springs in series), so the inverse (Reuss) rule applies. The result is dominated by the soft matrix.

questions.q: A steel has endurance limit 300 MPa and UTS 600 MPa. With a mean stress of 200 MPa, what alternating stress does the Goodman relation permit for infinite life?
Which index should be maximised to minimise the mass of a tie rod of fixed length that must have a specified axial stiffness?
questions.why: Stiffness S = EA/L. With A free, m = SL²ρ/E, so maximise E/ρ.

questions.q: Using %IC = 100[1 − exp(−0.25Δχ²)], estimate the ionic character of NaCl (χ_Na = 0.93, χ_Cl = 3.16) and MgO (χ_Mg = 1.31, χ_O = 3.44). Comment on the result.
markScheme: Comment: both predominantly ionic but with significant covalent character; bonding is mixed
questions.modelAnswer: For NaCl, Δχ = 3.16 − 0.93 = 2.23, so Δχ² = 4.97 and %IC = 100[1 − exp(−1.243)] ≈ 71%. For MgO, Δχ = 3.44 − 1.31 = 2.13, Δχ² = 4.54 and %IC = 100[1 − exp(−1.134)] ≈ 68%. Both compounds are mainly ionic, yet roughly 30% covalent character remains, so real ceramic bonds are mixed rather than purely ionic.

questions.q: Copper is FCC with atomic radius 0.128 nm and molar mass 63.55 g/mol. Calculate its lattice parameter and theoretical density (N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹).
questions.modelAnswer: For FCC, atoms touch along the face diagonal, so 4R = √2a and a = 2√2 × 0.128 = 0.362 nm = 3.62 × 10⁻⁸ cm. V_c = a³ = 4.75 × 10⁻²³ cm³. With 4 atoms per cell, ρ = (4 × 63.55)/(4.75 × 10⁻²³ × 6.022 × 10²³) = 254.2/28.6 ≈ 8.90 g/cm³. This is close to the measured 8.96 g/cm³.

questions.q: The vacancy formation energy in copper is 0.90 eV. Copper contains 8.4 × 10²⁸ atoms per m³ at 1000 °C. Estimate the equilibrium vacancy concentration at that temperature (k = 8.62 × 10⁻⁵ eV/K).
questions.modelAnswer: With T = 1273 K, kT = 8.62 × 10⁻⁵ × 1273 = 0.1097 eV. N_v/N = exp(−0.90/0.1097) = exp(−8.20) ≈ 2.7 × 10⁻⁴. So N_v ≈ 8.4 × 10²⁸ × 2.7 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 2.3 × 10²⁵ vacancies per m³, roughly one site in 3700 vacant.

questions.q: The theoretical shear strength of a perfect crystal is of order G/10 to G/30, yet pure metal single crystals yield at roughly G/10⁴ or less. Explain this discrepancy and why it matters for strengthening alloys.
markScheme: Theoretical estimate assumes a whole plane of bonds breaks simultaneously
Dislocation glide breaks and remakes bonds one line at a time, needing far lower stress
Hence strength is controlled by obstacles to dislocation motion
Strengthening mechanisms (solutes, grain boundaries, precipitates, forest dislocations) work by impeding glide
questions.modelAnswer: The theoretical estimate assumes one atomic plane slides rigidly over another, breaking every bond across the plane together. Real crystals contain dislocations. When a dislocation glides, only the bonds along its line rearrange at any instant, so slip needs a tiny fraction of the theoretical stress. Yield strength is therefore set by how easily dislocations move. Every practical strengthening method (solid solution, grain refinement, work hardening, precipitation) adds obstacles to their motion. Making near-perfect crystals, as in whiskers, approaches theoretical strength but is impractical for bulk parts.

questions.q: A steel has σ₀ = 70 MPa and Hall–Petch coefficient k = 0.74 MPa·m^½. Calculate its yield strength at a grain size of 25 µm, and state what happens if the grain size is reduced to 6.25 µm.
markScheme: At 6.25 µm, d^(−½) = 400 so σ_y = 366 MPa
questions.modelAnswer: σ_y = σ₀ + kd^(−½). For d = 25 × 10⁻⁶ m, d^(−½) = 200 m^(−½), so σ_y = 70 + 0.74 × 200 = 218 MPa. Cutting the grain size to a quarter doubles d^(−½) to 400 m^(−½), giving σ_y = 70 + 296 = 366 MPa. Grain refinement also tends to lower the ductile–brittle transition temperature.

questions.q: A Pb–40 wt% Sn alloy cools slowly from the melt. Using eutectic data (183 °C; L 61.9, α 18.3, β 97.8 wt% Sn), find (a) the fractions of primary α and liquid just above 183 °C, (b) the fractions of α and β just below 183 °C, and (c) the fraction of eutectic α.
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Just above 183 °C the tie line runs from α (18.3) to L (61.9). Primary α = (61.9 − 40)/(61.9 − 18.3) = 21.9/43.6 = 0.50 and liquid = 0.50. (b) Just below, the tie line runs from α (18.3) to β (97.8): W_α = 57.8/79.5 = 0.73 and W_β = 0.27. (c) All α beyond the primary α formed in the eutectic: 0.73 − 0.50 = 0.23. The eutectic microconstituent (0.50) is therefore 0.23 α and 0.27 β.

questions.q: Explain the difference between hardness and hardenability, and how the Jominy end-quench test distinguishes a plain carbon steel from a Cr–Mo low-alloy steel with the same carbon content.
markScheme: Hardness: resistance to indentation; maximum hardness depends mainly on carbon content
Hardenability: ability to form martensite to depth, i.e. at slower cooling rates
Jominy: bar quenched at one end, hardness measured along its length
Both steels have similar hardness at the quenched end; the alloy steel stays hard much further along the bar
questions.modelAnswer: Hardness is resistance to indentation. The maximum hardness of martensite depends mainly on carbon content. Hardenability describes how slow a cooling rate can still give martensite, and so how deep a section hardens. In the Jominy test a standard bar is austenitised, water-sprayed on one end, and hardness is measured along its length. Both steels reach similar hardness at the quenched end because they have the same carbon. Cr and Mo delay pearlite and bainite, so the alloy steel's curve stays high much further along the bar.

questions.q: A polyethylene sample has number-average molar mass 100 000 g/mol and density 0.940 g/cm³. Crystalline and amorphous PE have densities 1.00 and 0.855 g/cm³. Calculate the degree of polymerisation and percentage crystallinity (C = 12.01, H = 1.008 g/mol).

Silicon nitride test bars have Weibull modulus m = 10 and characteristic strength σ₀ = 300 MPa (for the test volume V₀). (a) Find the survival probability at 200 MPa and 250 MPa. (b) A component has twice the stressed volume of a test bar. Find its survival probability at 200 MPa. (c) What stress gives 99.9% survival for the test volume?
questions.modelAnswer: (a) P_s = exp[−(σ/σ₀)ᵐ]. At 200 MPa, (2/3)¹⁰ = 0.0173, so P_s = 0.983. At 250 MPa, (5/6)¹⁰ = 0.162, so P_s = 0.851. A 25% rise in stress increases failure probability almost ninefold. (b) With V/V₀ = 2, P_s = exp(−2 × 0.0173) = 0.966, equal to 0.983². (c) Setting P_s = 0.999 gives (σ/σ₀)¹⁰ = −ln 0.999 = 1.0005 × 10⁻³, so σ = 300 × (1.0005 × 10⁻³)^0.1 ≈ 150 MPa. Reliable design needs only half the characteristic strength.

questions.q: A component suffers 2 × 10⁴ cycles at a stress amplitude whose life is 1 × 10⁵ cycles, then 5 × 10⁴ cycles at a lower amplitude whose life is 4 × 10⁵ cycles. Using Miner's rule, find the damage fraction and the remaining cycles at the lower amplitude.
questions.modelAnswer: Miner's rule sums cycle ratios: D = 20 000/100 000 + 50 000/400 000 = 0.200 + 0.125 = 0.325. Failure is predicted at D = 1, leaving 0.675. At the lower amplitude, this corresponds to 0.675 × 4 × 10⁵ = 2.7 × 10⁵ further cycles. Miner's rule ignores sequence effects: for high-then-low sequences like this one, failure often occurs at Σn/N below 1, so the rule can be non-conservative.

questions.q: Use the Griffith equation to estimate the fracture stress of a glass plate (E = 70 GPa, surface energy 1.0 J/m²) containing an internal crack of half-length 1 µm, and explain why freshly drawn glass fibres are much stronger than window glass.
markScheme: Fresh fibres have fewer and smaller surface flaws; strength rises as a^(−½)
questions.modelAnswer: σ_f = √(2Eγ_s/πa) = √(2 × 70 × 10⁹ × 1.0/(π × 1 × 10⁻⁶)) = √(4.46 × 10¹⁶) ≈ 2.1 × 10⁸ Pa, so about 211 MPa. Window glass contains larger surface scratches, giving lower strength. Freshly drawn fibres have pristine surfaces with very small flaws, and because strength scales with a^(−½) they can be several times stronger until handling damages them.

questions.q: Derive the material index for a light, stiff beam of square cross-section (side b free) with specified length L and bending stiffness S = C₁EI/L³.
markScheme: Minimise mass by maximising M = E^½/ρ
questions.modelAnswer: For a square section, I = b⁴/12, so S = C₁Eb⁴/(12L³), giving b² = (12SL³/(C₁E))^½. The objective is mass, m = b²Lρ. Substituting eliminates the free variable: m = (12S/C₁)^½ L^(5/2) × ρ/E^½. S, L and C₁ are fixed by the design, so the lightest beam has the largest M = E^½/ρ.

questions.q:
The net potential energy of an ion pair in a hypothetical ionic solid is E(r) = −A/r + B/rⁿ, with A = 1.44 eV·nm and n = 8. The equilibrium separation is r₀ = 0.28 nm.

(a) Derive expressions for B and the bond energy E₀ in terms of A, n and r₀, and evaluate them. (b) Sketch and describe the force–separation curve and identify r₀ on it. (c) Explain how the depth, curvature and asymmetry of the energy well relate to the melting point, Young's modulus and thermal expansion coefficient. (d) Explain why a covalent solid such as diamond outperforms this ionic solid in stiffness, and why polyethylene is far less stiff than either.
markScheme: Force F = −dE/dr; F = 0 at r₀, attractive beyond, strongly repulsive below
Depth E₀ correlates with melting point
Curvature at r₀ gives bond stiffness; E ≈ S₀/r₀
Asymmetry causes thermal expansion; deep symmetric wells give low α
Diamond: directional covalent bonds in a 3D network, high curvature
Polyethylene: deformation stretches weak inter-chain secondary bonds, so low modulus
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) At equilibrium dE/dr = A/r₀² − nB/r₀ⁿ⁺¹ = 0, so B = A r₀ⁿ⁻¹/n = 1.44 × 0.28⁷/8 ≈ 2.43 × 10⁻⁵ eV·nm⁸. Substituting back gives E₀ = −A/r₀ + A/(n r₀) = −(A/r₀)(1 − 1/n). Here A/r₀ = 5.14 eV, so E₀ = −5.14 × 0.875 ≈ −4.5 eV.

(b) The force F = −dE/dr is zero at r₀. Beyond r₀ the net force is attractive, rising to a maximum (which sets the theoretical cohesive strength) and then decaying towards zero at large r. Below r₀ the repulsive term dominates and the force climbs very steeply because of the r⁻⁹ dependence. The slope of F at r₀ equals the bond stiffness.

(c) A deeper well (larger |E₀|) needs more thermal energy to separate atoms, so melting point rises with bond energy. The curvature S₀ = d²E/dr² at r₀ is the spring constant of the bond, and Young's modulus is roughly S₀/r₀. The well is steeper on the repulsive side, so as vibration amplitude grows with temperature the mean spacing moves outward. This asymmetry causes expansion, and deep, symmetric wells (e.g. strongly bonded ceramics) have low expansion coefficients.

(d) Diamond has a three-dimensional network of short, directional covalent bonds with very high curvature, so its modulus (about 1000 GPa) far exceeds most ionic solids. Polyethylene also contains C–C bonds, but only along its chains. In bulk loading, much of the strain is taken by the weak van der Waals bonds between chains, which have shallow, gently curved wells. Its modulus is therefore below about 1 GPa, unless the chains are highly aligned, as in drawn fibres.

questions.q:
Kestrel Instruments is checking a copper standard and an alloy single crystal.

(a) Copper is FCC with R = 0.128 nm. Calculate the lattice parameter, the (111) interplanar spacing and the diffraction angle 2θ for the first-order (111) reflection with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 0.1542 nm).
(b) Identify the slip planes and directions in FCC and state how many slip systems exist.
(c) A tensile load is applied to an FCC alloy single crystal. The active slip system's plane normal is at 60° to the load axis and its slip direction at 35°. The critical resolved shear stress is 12 MPa. Find the Schmid factor and the tensile stress at which slip begins.
(d) Explain why the yield stress of a polycrystal of the same alloy would be higher.
markScheme: Polycrystal: grains have different orientations, many with lower Schmid factors
Grain boundaries block dislocations and compatibility needs multiple slip (Taylor factor ~3, Hall–Petch)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) In FCC, atoms touch along the face diagonal, so a = 2√2R = 2√2 × 0.128 = 0.362 nm. The (111) spacing is d = a/√(1 + 1 + 1) = 0.362/1.732 = 0.209 nm. From Bragg's law with n = 1, sin θ = λ/(2d) = 0.1542/0.418 = 0.369, so θ = 21.6° and the peak appears at 2θ ≈ 43.3°, which matches the strong first copper peak seen in practice.

(b) Slip takes place on the close-packed {111} planes along the close-packed ⟨110⟩ directions. There are 4 distinct {111} planes, each containing 3 ⟨110⟩ directions, giving 12 slip systems. This large number, all active at low temperature, explains the good ductility and toughness of FCC metals.

(c) The Schmid factor is cos φ cos λ = cos 60° × cos 35° = 0.500 × 0.819 = 0.410. Slip starts when the resolved shear stress reaches the CRSS: σ = τ_CRSS/(cos φ cos λ) = 12/0.410 ≈ 29.3 MPa. The maximum possible Schmid factor is 0.5, so this orientation is fairly favourable.

(d) In a polycrystal each grain is differently oriented, so many grains have lower Schmid factors than the best single-crystal orientation. Grains must also deform compatibly with their neighbours, which needs at least five independent slip systems per grain. Averaging over orientations gives a Taylor factor of about 3 for FCC (σ_y ≈ 3.1τ_CRSS) compared with about 2 for an ideally oriented crystal. Grain boundaries also block dislocations, adding the Hall–Petch term kd^(−½). The polycrystal therefore yields at a markedly higher stress.

questions.q:
A 10.0 mm diameter steel test-piece with a 50.0 mm gauge length is tested in tension. It yields at 23.6 kN, reaches a maximum load of 35.3 kN at an engineering strain of 0.18, and fractures. The broken gauge length measures 61.5 mm and the neck diameter is 6.2 mm. E = 207 GPa.

Calculate: (a) the yield strength and UTS; (b) the percentage elongation and reduction of area; (c) the true stress and true strain at maximum load; (d) the modulus of resilience. (e) Assuming Hollomon behaviour and Considère's criterion, estimate the strain-hardening exponent n and strength coefficient K. (f) Explain why the engineering stress falls after maximum load even though the metal continues to strain-harden.
markScheme: After UTS deformation localises in the neck; area falls faster than hardening raises true stress
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) A₀ = π(5.0)² = 78.5 mm². Yield strength = 23 600/78.5 ≈ 300 MPa and UTS = 35 300/78.5 ≈ 449 MPa.

(b) Elongation = (61.5 − 50.0)/50.0 = 23%. Reduction of area = (A₀ − A_f)/A₀ = 1 − (6.2/10.0)² = 1 − 0.384 = 62%. These values indicate a ductile steel.

(c) Up to maximum load, deformation is uniform, so σ_T = σ(1 + ε) = 449 × 1.18 ≈ 530 MPa and ε_T = ln(1.18) = 0.166.

(d) U_r = σ_y²/2E = (300)²/(2 × 207 000) ≈ 0.22 MPa, i.e. 0.22 MJ/m³. This is the elastic energy stored per unit volume at yield.

(e) Considère's criterion, dσ_T/dε_T = σ_T, gives ε_T = n at necking for σ_T = Kε_Tⁿ, so n ≈ 0.17. Then K = 530/(0.166)^0.166. Since 0.166^0.166 = exp(0.166 ln 0.166) = exp(−0.298) = 0.742, K ≈ 714 MPa, roughly 710 MPa. Values of n between 0.1 and 0.3 are typical of ductile steels.

(f) Beyond the UTS, the rate at which strain hardening raises true stress can no longer offset the loss of cross-sectional area. Any slightly thinner region carries a higher stress, deforms more and thins further, so deformation localises in a neck. The load the specimen can carry falls, and engineering stress, based on the original area, drops. True stress in the neck keeps rising until fracture. The post-UTS fall is a geometric instability, not material softening.

questions.q: Evaluate the four main mechanisms for strengthening metals: solid solution strengthening, work hardening, grain refinement and precipitation hardening. For each, explain the dislocation mechanism, give an engineering example and identify any penalty in ductility, toughness or high-temperature stability. Conclude by recommending a strengthening route for a low-temperature structural steel for an offshore platform, justifying your choice with reference to the ductile-to-brittle transition.
markScheme: All mechanisms work by impeding dislocation glide
Solid solution: lattice strain fields of solute atoms pin dislocations; e.g. Cu–Zn brass, Mn in steels
Work hardening: dislocation density rises and tangles form; e.g. cold-drawn wire; lost on annealing and reduces ductility
Grain refinement: boundaries block slip, Hall–Petch σ_y = σ₀ + kd^(−½)
Grain refinement uniquely raises both strength and toughness and lowers DBTT
Precipitation: coherent particles cut, larger particles bypassed by Orowan looping; e.g. Al–Cu, Ni superalloys
Precipitation penalty: overageing at high temperature, possible loss of toughness
Most mechanisms raise DBTT in ferritic steels
Recommendation: fine-grained steel via controlled (thermomechanical) rolling with microalloying (Nb, V, Ti)
Justification: strength plus lower DBTT, good weldability with low carbon
questions.modelAnswer:
Every strengthening mechanism works by making it harder for dislocations to glide.

Solid solution strengthening: substitutional or interstitial solute atoms distort the lattice and their strain fields interact with dislocation stress fields, pinning them. Brass (Cu–Zn) and Mn or Si in ferritic steels are examples. The gain is moderate and stable at temperature, but large additions reduce ductility, and interstitial carbon and nitrogen raise the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (DBTT) of ferritic steel.

Work hardening: plastic deformation multiplies dislocations, which tangle and block each other. Cold-drawn steel wire and rolled copper sheet rely on it. Ductility falls, and the effect disappears when the metal recovers and recrystallises, so it is unsuitable for hot service or for welded regions.

Grain refinement: grain boundaries interrupt slip because neighbouring grains have different orientations. Dislocations pile up until stress nucleates slip in the next grain, so σ_y = σ₀ + kd^(−½). Uniquely, refining grains also improves toughness and lowers DBTT, because cleavage cracks must reorient at every boundary.

Precipitation hardening: fine, closely spaced particles are either cut (coherent, small) or bypassed by Orowan looping (larger, incoherent). Age-hardened Al–Cu alloys and γ′-strengthened nickel superalloys are examples. Strength can be very high, but overageing at elevated temperature coarsens precipitates, and some systems lose toughness.

Recommendation: an offshore platform in cold seas must resist brittle fracture, so DBTT must sit well below the minimum service temperature, and welds must not crack. The best route is a low-carbon steel with a fine grain size produced by thermomechanically controlled rolling, with microalloying additions such as Nb, V or Ti. Their fine carbonitrides pin austenite grain boundaries and add modest precipitation strengthening. Grain refinement supplies most of the strength while lowering DBTT, and low carbon keeps weldability good. Relying on carbon or heavy cold work would raise strength but at the expense of toughness.

questions.q:
A plain carbon steel containing 0.40 wt% C is cooled slowly from 900 °C. Use the Fe–Fe₃C diagram data: eutectoid at 0.76 wt% C and 727 °C; maximum carbon in ferrite 0.022 wt%; cementite 6.70 wt% C.

(a) Describe the microstructural changes during cooling from 900 °C to room temperature, naming phases and microconstituents. (b) Calculate the fractions of proeutectoid ferrite and pearlite just below 727 °C. (c) Calculate the total fractions of ferrite and cementite just below 727 °C. (d) Explain how the microstructure and properties would differ if the same steel were instead quenched into water from 850 °C, and why the phase diagram cannot predict this.
markScheme: Crossing A₃ (~800 °C), proeutectoid ferrite nucleates at austenite grain boundaries
At 727 °C remaining austenite transforms to pearlite
Water quench gives martensite (BCT, supersaturated, diffusionless)
Much harder and brittle, needs tempering
Phase diagram is equilibrium; it contains no kinetics, so TTT/CCT diagrams are needed
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) At 900 °C the steel is single-phase austenite (γ, FCC). On cooling it crosses the A₃ line, at about 800 °C for 0.40% C, into the α + γ field. Proeutectoid ferrite nucleates, mainly at austenite grain boundaries, and grows. Ferrite dissolves very little carbon, so the remaining austenite becomes richer, following the A₃ line towards 0.76% C. At 727 °C the remaining austenite, now of eutectoid composition, transforms to pearlite: alternating lamellae of ferrite and cementite. Further cooling to room temperature causes only negligible change.

(b) Just above 727 °C, the lever rule between ferrite (0.022) and austenite (0.76) gives the austenite fraction, which all becomes pearlite: W_p = (0.40 − 0.022)/(0.76 − 0.022) = 0.378/0.738 = 0.51. Proeutectoid ferrite = 0.49.

(c) Just below 727 °C, the tie line runs from ferrite (0.022) to cementite (6.70): W_α = (6.70 − 0.40)/(6.70 − 0.022) = 6.30/6.678 = 0.94 and W_Fe₃C = 0.06. Most of the ferrite (0.94 − 0.49 = 0.45) is therefore eutectoid ferrite inside the pearlite.

(d) Quenching from 850 °C (fully austenitic) cools the steel faster than the critical cooling rate, so carbon cannot diffuse to form ferrite and cementite. Austenite instead transforms by diffusionless shear to martensite: body-centred tetragonal iron supersaturated with carbon. Martensite in a 0.40% C steel is very hard, roughly 55–58 HRC when fully martensitic, but brittle, and quench stresses may cause distortion or cracking, so it would normally be tempered. The phase diagram shows only equilibrium states and contains no information on time. Martensite is a metastable, non-equilibrium phase, so its formation must be predicted from TTT or CCT diagrams, which add transformation kinetics.

questions.q: "An equilibrium phase diagram is the single most useful tool a materials engineer has, yet the microstructures of real engineering components rarely match its predictions." Discuss this proposition with reference to casting, welding and heat treatment of engineering alloys.
markScheme: Explains what phase diagrams provide: phases, compositions, fractions (lever rule), invariant reactions, solubility limits
Uses: alloy design, solder choice (eutectic), heat-treatment windows such as solution treatment
Equilibrium assumes slow cooling and complete diffusion
Casting: coring and non-equilibrium eutectic in nominally single-phase alloys; segregation; Scheil behaviour
Welding: steep thermal gradients, heat-affected zone grain growth, martensite in HAZ of hardenable steels
Heat treatment deliberately exploits non-equilibrium: martensite, bainite, supersaturated solid solutions, metastable precipitates (GP zones, θ′)
Fe₃C itself is metastable relative to graphite
Need for kinetic tools: TTT/CCT diagrams, diffusion distance √(Dt)
Balanced conclusion: diagram is the essential reference frame for interpreting departures, not a full prediction
Uses specific data or examples accurately
questions.modelAnswer:
Equilibrium phase diagrams state which phases are thermodynamically stable at each composition and temperature, their compositions (tie lines) and amounts (lever rule), and where invariant reactions occur. They underpin alloy design. Eutectic Pb–Sn and Sn–Ag–Cu solders are chosen for their low, single melting point. Solution-treatment temperatures for Al–Cu alloys are read from the single-phase α field, and steel austenitising temperatures from the A₃ and A₁ lines. In that sense the proposition's first half is fair.

However, the diagram assumes enough time for complete diffusion, which real processes seldom give.

Casting: solid-state diffusion lags behind solidification, so isomorphous alloys such as Cu–Ni form cored dendrites, with the first solid richer in the high-melting component. In eutectic systems, alloys whose overall composition lies outside the eutectic range can still contain some non-equilibrium eutectic between dendrites, as the Scheil model predicts. Macrosegregation and porosity further depart from the diagram. Homogenisation anneals are used to approach equilibrium.

Welding: heating and cooling are extremely fast and gradients steep. The heat-affected zone of a hardenable steel can be cooled through austenite fast enough to form martensite, causing hydrogen cracking. Near the fusion line grains coarsen. None of this appears on the Fe–C diagram.

Heat treatment: here engineers exploit departures from equilibrium. Quenched martensite, bainite and the supersaturated α in age-hardenable aluminium are non-equilibrium states, and the strengthening precipitates (GP zones, θ″, θ′) are metastable stages before equilibrium θ. Cementite itself is metastable with respect to graphite.

Predicting these structures needs kinetic tools: TTT and CCT diagrams, diffusion distances of order √(Dt), and nucleation theory.

The proposition is therefore largely right but misleading if read as a criticism. The phase diagram is not meant to predict real microstructures; it defines the equilibrium reference against which all departures are understood. Coring, martensite and age hardening can only be explained by knowing what equilibrium would have been. The best view is that the diagram is necessary but not sufficient: it must be combined with kinetics.

questions.q:
Harlow Gears must case-carburise a steel gear containing 0.20 wt% C. The furnace atmosphere holds the surface at 1.00 wt% C. The specification requires 0.50 wt% C at a depth of 0.50 mm. For carbon in austenite, D₀ = 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s and Q = 148 kJ/mol (R = 8.314 J/mol·K). erf(0.627) ≈ 0.625.

(a) Calculate the diffusion coefficient at 1000 °C and 900 °C. (b) Calculate the carburising time at 1000 °C. (c) Find the time needed at 900 °C to achieve the same profile. (d) Discuss the trade-off between the two temperatures, and explain the role of quenching and tempering after carburising.
markScheme: D = D₀exp(−Q/RT) with T in K
Same profile needs same Dt: t(900 °C) = t × D₁₂₇₃/D₁₁₇₃ ≈ 2.3 × 3.29 ≈ 7.5 h
Higher T: faster but grain coarsening and distortion, furnace wear
Lower T: finer grains, but longer cycle and cost
Quench from austenite gives high-carbon martensitic case on tough lower-carbon core
Low-temperature temper relieves stress, reduces brittleness, retains surface hardness
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) D = D₀exp(−Q/RT). At 1000 °C (1273 K): Q/RT = 148 000/(8.314 × 1273) = 13.98, so D = 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ × 8.45 × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 1.94 × 10⁻¹¹ m²/s. At 900 °C (1173 K): Q/RT = 15.18, so D ≈ 5.9 × 10⁻¹² m²/s. The diffusivity is about 3.3 times higher at the higher temperature.

(b) The erf solution gives (C_x − C₀)/(C_s − C₀) = (0.50 − 0.20)/(1.00 − 0.20) = 0.375 = 1 − erf(z), so erf(z) = 0.625 and z = x/(2√(Dt)) = 0.627. Rearranging: t = [x/(2z)]²/D = (0.50 × 10⁻³/1.254)²/(1.94 × 10⁻¹¹) = (3.99 × 10⁻⁴)²/(1.94 × 10⁻¹¹) ≈ 8.2 × 10³ s, about 2.3 h.

(c) The same concentration profile requires the same value of Dt. So t₉₀₀ = t₁₀₀₀ × D₁₀₀₀/D₉₀₀ = 2.27 h × 3.29 ≈ 7.5 h.

(d) Carburising at 1000 °C cuts cycle time by over two-thirds, increasing furnace throughput. However, austenite grains coarsen more at higher temperature, which reduces core toughness and fatigue performance unless the steel is grain-refined (e.g. Al- or Nb-treated). Distortion and furnace maintenance also increase. At 900 °C grains stay finer and distortion is lower, at the cost of longer cycles and higher energy per batch. The choice depends on steel grade, part size and production volume.

After carburising, the gear is quenched from the austenite field. The high-carbon case transforms to hard martensite for wear and contact fatigue resistance, while the 0.20% C core forms tougher, lower-carbon structures. Compressive residual stresses develop in the case, improving bending fatigue life. A low-temperature temper (typically around 150–200 °C) then relieves quench stresses and reduces brittleness while keeping high surface hardness.

questions.q:
Wren Aero uses an Al–4 wt% Cu alloy for a brazed bracket. A batch has been accidentally held for several hours at a temperature well above its normal ageing temperature after correct solution treatment and quenching. Its hardness is well below specification.

(a) Describe the three stages of a correct precipitation-hardening treatment and explain the purpose of each with reference to the Al–Cu phase diagram. (b) Describe the precipitation sequence and explain why hardness rises to a peak and then falls. (c) Diagnose the batch's problem and state how it can be rectified. (d) Explain why age-hardened aluminium alloys are generally unsuitable for long-term service at elevated temperature.
markScheme: Solution treat in single-phase α field (above solvus, below eutectic/solidus) to dissolve Cu
Quench to retain supersaturated solid solution and excess vacancies
Age (natural or artificial) to precipitate fine particles
Sequence: GP zones → θ″ → θ′ → θ (CuAl₂)
Peak: fine, closely spaced coherent/semi-coherent precipitates strongly impede dislocations
Overageing: coarsening, loss of coherency, wider spacing, Orowan bypass easier, hardness falls
Rectify: re-solution treat, quench and age correctly
High-temperature service causes continued coarsening and overageing; strength falls with time
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Solution treatment heats the alloy into the single-phase α field, above the solvus but below the temperature at which liquid forms, so the copper dissolves fully. Quenching rapidly to room temperature prevents equilibrium θ forming, leaving a supersaturated solid solution with excess vacancies that later speed diffusion. Ageing, either at room temperature (natural) or at a moderately raised temperature (artificial), lets copper cluster and precipitate as a fine dispersion.

(b) The sequence is supersaturated α → GP zones (copper-rich discs one or two atomic layers thick) → θ″ → θ′ → equilibrium θ (CuAl₂). Early precipitates are coherent with the matrix and surrounded by strain fields. As they grow and become more numerous, they resist dislocations more strongly, either by being sheared or, once larger, by forcing dislocations to bow between them (Orowan mechanism). Peak hardness corresponds to a dense distribution of θ″ and θ′. With further time, larger particles grow at the expense of smaller ones, coherency is lost and spacing widens, so dislocations bypass them easily and hardness falls: overageing.

(c) Holding the batch for hours well above the normal ageing temperature has driven it past peak into the overaged condition, with coarse θ′ and θ. Further ageing cannot recover strength because coarsening is irreversible. The parts must be solution treated again to redissolve the copper, quenched, and then aged correctly, with checks on hardness and distortion. The brazed joint must also tolerate the solution-treatment temperature; if it cannot, the batch should be scrapped.

(d) Strengthening relies on a metastable precipitate distribution. At elevated service temperatures, diffusion continues, so precipitates coarsen with time and the alloy slowly overages, losing strength. Aluminium also has a low melting point, so even moderate temperatures are a significant fraction of T_m. For sustained heat, titanium alloys or steels are used instead.

questions.q:
Fulmar Bikes is designing a unidirectional carbon fibre/epoxy seat stay. Fibres: E_f = 230 GPa, tensile strength 3.5 GPa, diameter 7 µm. Epoxy: E_m = 3.5 GPa. Fibre volume fraction 0.60. Fibre–matrix interfacial shear strength 50 MPa. Densities: fibre 1.80 Mg/m³, epoxy 1.20 Mg/m³.

(a) Calculate the longitudinal and transverse moduli. (b) Calculate the fraction of an axial load carried by the fibres. (c) Calculate the composite density and its specific longitudinal stiffness, and compare with aluminium (E = 70 GPa, ρ = 2.70 Mg/m³). (d) Calculate the critical fibre length and comment on its significance for a chopped-fibre alternative. (e) Advise on ply orientation if the stay sees bending plus some torsion.
markScheme: E/ρ ≈ 89 versus Al ≈ 26 GPa per Mg/m³
Chopped fibres should be well above l_c, ideally over about 15 l_c, to be efficient; short fibres give lower stiffness and strength
Anisotropy: transverse stiffness about 1/16 of longitudinal
Use mainly 0° plies for bending with ±45° plies for torsional (shear) stiffness, balanced and symmetric layup
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Longitudinal (iso-strain): E_∥ = V_fE_f + V_mE_m = 0.6 × 230 + 0.4 × 3.5 = 138 + 1.4 = 139 GPa. Transverse (iso-stress): 1/E_⊥ = 0.6/230 + 0.4/3.5 = 0.00261 + 0.1143 = 0.1169, so E_⊥ ≈ 8.6 GPa.

(b) Under iso-strain, each constituent carries load in proportion to V·E. Fibre share = 138/139.4 ≈ 0.99: the fibres carry about 99% of the axial load, and the matrix mainly transfers load and stabilises the fibres.

(c) ρ_c = 0.6 × 1.80 + 0.4 × 1.20 = 1.56 Mg/m³. Specific stiffness E/ρ = 139.4/1.56 ≈ 89 GPa per Mg/m³, compared with 70/2.70 ≈ 26 for aluminium: about 3.4 times higher along the fibres. Transversely (8.6/1.56 ≈ 5.5) the composite is far worse than aluminium.

(d) l_c = σ_fd/(2τ_c) = (3500 × 7 × 10⁻⁶)/(2 × 50) m = 2.45 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.245 mm. Shear stress at the interface builds fibre stress from each end, so a fibre shorter than l_c never reaches its full strength. For efficient reinforcement chopped fibres should be much longer than l_c, roughly 15 l_c or more (about 4 mm). Even then, random short fibres give much lower stiffness and strength than continuous aligned fibres, so they suit low-cost moulded parts rather than a structural stay.

(e) The 16-fold anisotropy shows a purely unidirectional stay would be weak and floppy off-axis. Bending stresses run along the stay, so 0° plies should dominate the outer layers where bending stress is highest. Torsion creates shear, best resisted by fibres at ±45°, so a proportion of ±45° plies should be included. A balanced, symmetric layup (e.g. [0/±45/0]s) avoids warping and bend–twist coupling, and a few 90° plies help resist crushing at clamps and dropouts.

questions.q:
A large steel plate in a crane structure contains a through-thickness edge crack 1.0 mm deep, detected at inspection. It sees constant-amplitude loading from 0 to 150 MPa (R = 0). Take Y = 1 throughout. Paris law constants: C = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ (da/dN in m/cycle, ΔK in MPa√m), m = 3. K_IC = 50 MPa√m.

(a) Calculate the critical crack length. (b) Integrate the Paris law to estimate the number of cycles to failure. (c) Estimate how many cycles it takes for the crack to grow from 1 mm to 5 mm, and comment. (d) Repeat (a) and (b) if the stress range doubles to 0–300 MPa, and comment on the sensitivity of life to stress. (e) Recommend an inspection strategy.
markScheme: 1 to 5 mm takes ≈ 1.86 × 10⁵ cycles, about two-thirds of life
Most life spent while crack is small; growth accelerates
At 300 MPa, a_c ≈ 8.8 mm and N ≈ 2.8 × 10⁴ cycles
Doubling stress range cuts life about tenfold (2³ = 8 from Paris, plus smaller a_c)
Inspection interval set from crack growth between detectable size and a_c, with safety factor (e.g. half the remaining life), damage-tolerant approach
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Fast fracture occurs when K_max = Yσ_max√(πa) = K_IC. So a_c = (1/π)(K_IC/σ_max)² = (1/π)(50/150)² = 0.1111/π = 0.0354 m, or 35.4 mm.

(b) With ΔK = Δσ√(πa), da/dN = C(Δσ)³(π)^(3/2)a^(3/2). Separating variables, N = [1/(C(Δσ√π)³)] ∫a^(−3/2) da from a₀ to a_c = 2(a₀^(−½) − a_c^(−½))/[C(Δσ√π)³].
Δσ√π = 150 × 1.7725 = 265.9, and its cube is 1.88 × 10⁷. a₀^(−½) = (0.001)^(−½) = 31.62 and a_c^(−½) = (0.0354)^(−½) = 5.32 (units m^(−½)). N = 2 × 26.30/(1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.88 × 10⁷) = 52.6/1.88 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 2.8 × 10⁵ cycles.

(c) From 1 to 5 mm: a^(−½) changes from 31.62 to 14.14, so N = 2 × 17.48/(1.88 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 1.86 × 10⁵ cycles, about two-thirds of the total life. Growth accelerates as the crack lengthens, so most life is used while the crack is small, and the final stages are rapid.

(d) At 0–300 MPa, a_c = (1/π)(50/300)² = 8.8 mm. Δσ√π = 531.7, cube 1.50 × 10⁸. a_c^(−½) = 10.63, so N = 2(31.62 − 10.63)/(1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.50 × 10⁸) = 41.98/1.50 × 10⁻³ ≈ 2.8 × 10⁴ cycles. Doubling the stress range cuts life by about a factor of ten: a factor of 2³ = 8 from the Paris exponent, and more because the critical crack is smaller. Life is highly sensitive to stress, so overloads and stress concentrations matter greatly.

(e) Use a damage-tolerant approach. Establish the smallest crack the chosen NDT method (e.g. ultrasonic or magnetic particle) reliably detects, compute the cycles to grow from that size to a_c, and inspect at a fraction of that interval (commonly half or less), so a crack missed once is caught before failure. Monitor actual load spectra and repair or replace when cracks are found.

questions.q:
Osprey Turbines is assessing a nickel superalloy for a turbine disc rim. Rupture tests give a life of 1000 h at 600 °C under the design stress. Steady-state creep tests at 600 °C show that raising the stress by 50% increases the creep rate from 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ s⁻¹ to 1.35 × 10⁻⁷ s⁻¹. At constant stress, the creep rate increases by a factor of 10 when temperature rises from 550 °C to 600 °C.

(a) Using a Larson–Miller constant of 20, find the rupture life at 650 °C under the same stress. (b) Determine the stress exponent n and identify the probable creep mechanism. (c) Estimate the creep activation energy (R = 8.314 J/mol·K). (d) Critically discuss the reliability of these extrapolations and explain the microstructural features used to give nickel superalloys their creep resistance.
markScheme: Comparable to self-diffusion activation energy in Ni
Extrapolation risks: mechanism change at different stress/T, microstructural instability (γ′ coarsening), oxidation, constant C assumption, scatter
γ′ Ni₃(Al,Ti) coherent precipitates, solid solution strengtheners (W, Mo, Re, Co)
Grain boundary engineering: carbides, directional solidification or single crystals (blades), coatings
Reasoned conclusion on design use with safety factors and long-term testing
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) At 600 °C (873 K), P = 873(20 + log 1000) = 873 × 23 = 20 079. At 650 °C (923 K) with the same stress, P is unchanged: log t_r = 20 079/923 − 20 = 21.754 − 20 = 1.754, so t_r ≈ 57 h. A 50 K rise cuts life by a factor of about 18.

(b) ε̇ ∝ σⁿ at constant T, so n = ln(ε̇₂/ε̇₁)/ln(σ₂/σ₁) = ln(6.75)/ln(1.5) = 1.910/0.405 ≈ 4.7. An exponent of about 4–5 is typical of dislocation (power-law) creep, controlled by climb, rather than diffusional creep (n ≈ 1).

(c) At constant stress, ε̇ ∝ exp(−Q/RT), so ln 10 = (Q/R)(1/823 − 1/873). The bracket is 6.96 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹, so Q = 8.314 × 2.303/6.96 × 10⁻⁵ ≈ 2.75 × 10⁵ J/mol, about 275 kJ/mol. This is of the same order as lattice self-diffusion in nickel, consistent with climb-controlled creep.

(d) These estimates rest on assumptions. The Larson–Miller constant varies between alloys, and a single value of 20 is approximate. Extrapolating to longer lives or different temperatures assumes the same mechanism operates. At lower stresses diffusional or grain-boundary creep may dominate, and at higher temperature γ′ precipitates coarsen or dissolve, so the microstructure itself changes. Oxidation and hot corrosion add environmental damage that short tests underestimate. Rupture data also show significant scatter. Designers therefore use lower-bound data, safety factors on life and stress, and long-term confirmation tests, and avoid extrapolating more than about a factor of three in time.

Nickel superalloys resist creep because of a high volume fraction of coherent γ′ (Ni₃(Al,Ti)) precipitates in the FCC γ matrix. Dislocations must cut these ordered particles, creating antiphase boundaries, or climb around them, which is slow. Refractory solutes such as W, Mo and Re add solid-solution strengthening and slow diffusion. Grain-boundary carbides and small boron or zirconium additions resist boundary sliding. In blades, directional solidification removes transverse boundaries and single crystals eliminate them entirely, while thermal barrier coatings lower metal temperature. For a disc, polycrystalline powder-metallurgy alloys balance creep with the fatigue strength a fine grain gives.

questions.q:
Merlin Drones needs a lightweight boom: a beam of fixed length loaded in bending, which must meet a specified bending stiffness. Its square cross-section dimensions may vary. Candidate data:

Steel: E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7.85 Mg/m³, £1.0/kg
Aluminium alloy: E = 69 GPa, ρ = 2.70 Mg/m³, £3.0/kg
Titanium alloy: E = 114 GPa, ρ = 4.43 Mg/m³, £25/kg
CFRP (quasi-isotropic): E = 100 GPa, ρ = 1.55 Mg/m³, £40/kg

(a) State the function, objective, constraints and free variable. (b) Using the index for a light, stiff beam, rank the materials and give each boom's mass relative to steel. (c) Rank them by cost for the same stiffness, relative to steel. (d) Recommend a material, discussing trade-offs and factors outside the index.
markScheme: Constraints: specified stiffness, fixed length; free variable: section size
M = E^½/ρ: steel 1.85, Al 3.08, Ti 2.41, CFRP 6.45
Relative mass ∝ 1/M: Al 0.60, Ti 0.77, CFRP 0.29 of steel
Ranking for mass: CFRP > Al > Ti > steel
Cost index C_mρ/E^½: steel 0.54, Al 0.98, Ti 10.4, CFRP 6.2
Recommendation: CFRP if mass critical (drone endurance), Al as low-cost alternative; Ti dominated
Other factors: shape (tubes), joining, damage tolerance/impact, manufacturing, recyclability, availability
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Function: a beam loaded in bending. Objective: minimise mass, because mass reduces flight endurance. Constraints: specified bending stiffness and fixed length. Free variable: the cross-section size b.

(b) For a light, stiff beam, maximise M = E^½/ρ (E in GPa, ρ in Mg/m³). Steel: √210/7.85 = 14.49/7.85 = 1.85. Aluminium: √69/2.70 = 8.31/2.70 = 3.08. Titanium: √114/4.43 = 10.68/4.43 = 2.41. CFRP: √100/1.55 = 10/1.55 = 6.45. Mass is proportional to 1/M, so relative to steel: aluminium 1.85/3.08 = 0.60, titanium 0.77, CFRP 0.29. The ranking is CFRP, aluminium, titanium, steel. A CFRP boom weighs under a third of a steel one, and aluminium beats titanium despite titanium's higher modulus.

(c) Cost per stiffness scales with C_mρ/E^½. Steel: 1.0 × 7.85/14.49 = 0.54. Aluminium: 3.0 × 2.70/8.31 = 0.98. Titanium: 25 × 4.43/10.68 = 10.4. CFRP: 40 × 1.55/10 = 6.2. Relative to steel: aluminium 1.8, CFRP 11.5, titanium 19. Steel is cheapest, then aluminium.

(d) Titanium is dominated: heavier and more expensive than aluminium and costlier than CFRP. The real choice lies between CFRP (lightest, about half the mass of aluminium) and aluminium (lightest at moderate cost). For a drone, every gram saved extends flight time or payload, and boom material cost is small compared with the whole aircraft, so CFRP tube is recommended for a performance product. Aluminium tube suits a budget model.

The index ignores several factors. A thin-walled tube shape improves efficiency for both materials, and the comparison holds for a given shape. CFRP has poor impact resistance and can hide damage, so crash durability, inspection and repair matter. Joining CFRP to motor mounts needs bonded or clamped joints. The quasi-isotropic modulus assumed is lower than a tailored layup could give. Aluminium is easier to recycle and machine, which matters for sustainability and small production runs.

questions.q:
Sandpiper Gas is selecting a steel for a thin-walled pressure vessel (radius 1.0 m, wall thickness 10 mm). The vessel must be safe against unstable fracture from cracks that might escape inspection. Two candidate steels are offered:

Steel X: σ_y = 1000 MPa, K_IC = 60 MPa√m
Steel Y: σ_y = 500 MPa, K_IC = 150 MPa√m

Take K = σ√(πa) for a crack in the wall, and hoop stress σ = pR/t.

(a) Explain the yield-before-break and leak-before-break criteria and derive the associated material indices. (b) For each steel, calculate the critical crack length at a stress equal to the yield strength, and evaluate the yield-before-break and leak-before-break indices. (c) For each steel, find the maximum pressure for leak-before-break (i) from the material-index result, assuming the wall is sized so that the hoop stress equals σ_y, and (ii) for the actual 10 mm wall. (d) Compare these with the pressures each steel could carry if limited only by yield. Make and justify a recommendation.
markScheme: Yield-before-break: vessel yields (visibly) before a crack of size a_c becomes critical; at σ = σ_y need a_c = (1/π)(K_IC/σ_y)² large, so maximise K_IC/σ_y

Leak-before-break: a crack must grow through the wall and leak before it becomes unstable; Ashby's simplification takes a through crack of total length equal to the wall thickness t (half-length a = t/2) at the design stress
With σ = σ_y and t = pR/σ_y, σ_y√(πt/2) = K_IC gives p = (2/π)K_IC²/(Rσ_y), so maximise K_IC²/σ_y

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) In yield-before-break, the vessel should yield, giving visible distortion, before any crack escaping inspection can cause fast fracture. At σ = σ_y the critical crack is a_c = (1/π)(K_IC/σ_y)², so a tolerant material maximises K_IC/σ_y. In leak-before-break, a crack growing through the wall should leak, so it can be detected, before it becomes unstable. Ashby's simplified form requires a through-wall crack whose total length equals the wall thickness t (half-length a = t/2) to be stable at the working stress, giving σ√(πt/2) = K_IC. With σ = pR/t and the wall sized so that σ is at most σ_y (t = pR/σ_y), this leads to p = (2/π)K_IC²/(Rσ_y). For a given vessel radius, maximising K_IC²/σ_y maximises the pressure for which leak-before-break holds.

(b) Steel X: a_c = (1/π)(60/1000)² = 1.15 × 10⁻³ m, about 1.1 mm. Steel Y: a_c = (1/π)(150/500)² = 0.0286 m, about 28.6 mm. Indices: K_IC/σ_y is 0.06 m^½ for X and 0.30 m^½ for Y. K_IC²/σ_y is 3.6 MPa·m for X and 45 MPa·m for Y.

(c)(i) With the wall sized so that σ = σ_y, p_LBB = (2/π)K_IC²/(Rσ_y). X: (2/π) × 3.6/1.0 = 2.3 MPa (a 2.3 mm wall). Y: (2/π) × 45/1.0 = 28.6 MPa (a 57 mm wall). (ii) For the actual 10 mm wall, leak-before-break needs σ√(π × 0.005) ≤ K_IC, i.e. σ ≤ K_IC/0.125. X: σ ≤ 479 MPa, so p ≤ 479 × 0.010/1.0 ≈ 4.8 MPa. Y: σ ≤ 1197 MPa, above its yield strength, so leak-before-break holds at any pressure up to yield.

(d) If limited only by yield, p = σ_yt/R = σ_y × 0.010/1.0. X carries 10 MPa and Y 5 MPa. Steel X looks twice as good on strength alone, but at 10 MPa its wall stress approaches 1000 MPa, where a 1.1 mm crack (hard to find reliably by inspection) is critical, and in this wall leak-before-break holds only up to about 4.8 MPa. It would fail catastrophically without warning. Steel Y's 5 MPa yield-limited pressure is well inside its leak-before-break limit, and it tolerates cracks nearly 30 mm long, easily found by routine NDT.

Recommendation: choose steel Y. If more pressure is needed, increase wall thickness rather than use the stronger, brittle steel. Steel X is only acceptable at much lower pressure with very sensitive inspection. Safety-critical vessels follow fail-safe design: toughness matters more than strength.
